questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with multiple comorbidities is admitted to a hospital ward where an outbreak of MRSA has been reported. As part of the infection control team, you are tasked with implementing the most effective measure to control the spread of MRSA. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step?

options.label: A
options.text: Prophylactic administration of vancomycin to all patients

options.label: C
options.text: Mandating the use of masks before invasive procedures

options.label: D
options.text: Ensuring rigorous hand hygiene before and after patient contact

questions.answerText: Ensuring rigorous hand hygiene before and after patient contact
questions.solutionHtml:
tify"> 

Option A: Prophylactic administration of vancomycin to all patients - This is not the most appropriate initial step for controlling MRSA. Prophylactic use of antibiotics should be reserved for specific clinical indications and should not be used as a routine measure for infection control due to the risk of antibiotic resistance.

 

Option B: Regular fumigation of the ward - Fumigation may help control some pathogens, but it is not the most effective initial step for controlling MRSA. Direct hand and surface contact are more common routes of transmission for MRSA.

 

Option C: Mandating the use of masks before invasive procedures - While the use of masks is important for preventing the spread of infections during invasive procedures, it is not the most appropriate initial step in controlling MRSA. Hand hygiene is a more fundamental measure.


Educational Objective:

 

MRSA is primarily transmitted through direct contact with contaminated hands or surfaces. Proper hand hygiene, including handwashing with soap and water or using alcohol-based hand sanitizers, is crucial in preventing the transmission of MRSA. 

 

Ref: Apurva Sastry Essentials of Medical Microbiology HIC Book 



Apurva Sastry Essentials of Medical Microbiology HIC Book

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with a diabetic foot ulcer presents to the clinic. He was previously treated with methicillin for a suspected Staphylococcus aureus infection. However, his condition has not improved, and a subsequent culture and sensitivity test indicate methicillin resistance. Which of the following antibiotics should be avoided in the treatment of this patient's infection due to likely resistance?
questions.solutionHtml:
n style="font-family:Aptos,sans-serif">Explanation:

 

Option A: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (Co-trimoxazole) - This antibiotic combination is often effective against MRSA and can be a suitable choice for treating MRSA infections.

 

Option C: Vancomycin - Vancomycin is a commonly used antibiotic for MRSA infections. It is effective against MRSA and is considered the drug of choice for serious MRSA infections.

 

Option D: Ciprofloxacin - Ciprofloxacin is a fluoroquinolone antibiotic and is generally not used as the first-line treatment for MRSA infections. Vancomycin or other suitable agents are preferred for MRSA.

 

Educational Objective:

 

While, Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and vancomycin are both suitable choices for treating MRSA infections. Vancomycin is the preferred antibiotic for treating methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) infections

 

Ref: Apurva Sastry Essentials of Medical Microbiologypg 66/4e

questions.stem: A laboratory scientist is presented with two bacterial isolates from a skin infection. Both are gram-positive cocci, but it is critical to determine whether the isolates are Staphylococcus spp. or Micrococcus spp. to guide treatment effectively. Which test would best differentiate between these two genera?
questions.solutionHtml:
="font-size:12.0pt">Option A: The catalase test can differentiate staphylococci (catalase-positive) from streptococci (catalase-negative), but both Micrococcus and Staphylococcus are catalase-positive.

 

Option C: Gram staining differentiates bacteria based on cell wall properties; however, both Micrococcus and Staphylococcus are gram-positive cocci, so this test would not distinguish between them.

 

Option D: The coagulase test is used to differentiate Staphylococcus aureus (which is coagulase-positive) from other Staphylococcus species, but not from Micrococcus.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Modified oxidase test is the most effective method for distinguishing between the genera Micrococcus and Staphylococcus, with Micrococcus being modified oxidase-positive and Staphylococcus being oxidase-negative. 

 

Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology 1/e p211



Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology 1/e p211

questions.stem: Following a series of surgeries in a postoperative ward, an outbreak of surgical site infections is noted. Cultures from the wound discharge of affected patients reveal coagulase-positive gram-positive cocci resistant to methicillin. A healthcare worker is identified as a nasal carrier of the same resistant strain. In controlling this outbreak, which of the following statements is correct regarding the characteristics of the pathogen responsible for the infections?

options.label: A
options.text: The primary mode of transmission in the outbreak is airborne.

options.label: B
options.text: The resistance to methicillin is due to the mecB gene.

options.label: C
options.text: The pathogen carries an altered penicillin-binding protein, leading to methicillin resistance.

options.label: D
options.text: The organism would be sensitive to amoxicillin-clavulanic acid.

questions.answerText: The pathogen carries an altered penicillin-binding protein, leading to methicillin resistance.
questions.solutionHtml:
pan style="font-size:12.0pt;">Option A. The primary mode of transmission in the outbreak is likely airborne: This statement is inconsistent with the mode of transmission of Staphylococcus aureus, which is typically through direct contact with contaminated hands or surfaces. Airborne transmission is not a common route for this pathogen in terms of causing surgical site infections.

 

Option B. The resistance to methicillin is due to the mecB gene: This statement is incorrect. Methicillin resistance is primarily mediated by the mecA gene, which is located on a staphylococcal chromosomal cassette (SCC).

 

Option D. The organism typically be sensitive to amoxicillin-clavulanic acid: This statement is incorrect because methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) strains are typically not sensitive to beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor combinations like amoxicillin-clavulanic acid due to the resistance conferred by altered PBPs and the presence of the mecA gene

 

Educational Objective:

 

Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is characterized by resistance to methicillin and other beta-lactam antibiotics due to the presence of the mecA gene, which encodes an altered penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a). MRSA primarily spreads through direct contact, especially in healthcare settings. 

 

Detection of MRSA

 

  1. Antimicrobial susceptibility test: Disk diffusion test can be done by using cefoxitin or oxacillin disks
  2. PCR detecting mecA gene
  3. Latex agglutination test detecting PBP-2a

 

Ref: Apurva Sastry Essentials of Medical Microbiology Essentials of Medical Microbiologypg66/4e



Apurva Sastry Essentials of Medical Microbiology Essentials of Medical Microbiologypg66/4e

questions.stem: A 70-year-old male with a history of valve replacement surgery presents with a new heart murmur and fever 12 months post-operation. His blood cultures are positive, suggesting infective endocarditis. Which organism is most commonly associated with late-onset prosthetic valve endocarditis?
questions.solutionHtml:
ridans

 

Explanation:  

 

Streptococcus viridans is identified as the most commonly associated organism with late-onset prosthetic valve endocarditis (PVE). This group of bacteria is part of the normal oral and respiratory flora and is known for causing subacute endocarditis, particularly in individuals with predisposing heart conditions or prosthetic heart valves. The late-onset nature of the infection suggests a more indolent course, which aligns with the pathogenic behavior of S. viridans, allowing it to adhere to and colonize prosthetic materials over time. 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Staphylococcus aureus: While S. aureus is a common cause of native valve endocarditis and can be associated with early-onset PVE (occurring within 12 months of surgery), it is less commonly associated with late-onset PVE compared to coagulase-negative staphylococci like S. epidermidis.

 

Option C. Staphylococcus epidermidis: S. epidermidis is a coagulase-negative Staphylococcus species frequently linked to early -onset PVE due to its ability to form biofilms on prosthetic devices. 

 

Option D. HACEK group bacteria: The HACEK group are commonly associated with endocarditis but less associated with prosthetic valve endocarditis.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Streptococcus viridans is the most commonly associated organism with late-onset prosthetic valve endocarditis, particularly due to its ability to cause subacute infections in individuals with prosthetic heart valves.

questions.stem: A patient presents to the clinic with severe abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea. Upon examination, the patient is found to have necrotic lesions in the intestine. Which organism is most commonly associated with this presentation, known as gastrointestinal enteritis necroticans?
questions.solutionHtml:
ly:Aptos,sans-serif">Explanation:

 

Option A: Clostridium difficile is associated with antibiotic-associated diarrhea and pseudomembranous colitis, not enteritis necroticans.

 

Option C: Clostridium botulinum is associated with botulism, a form of food poisoning that affects the nervous system.

 

Option D: Campylobacter jejuni is a common cause of bacterial gastroenteritis but does not typically cause enteritis necroticans.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Clostridium perfringens as the causative agent of gastrointestinal enteritis necroticans, a serious intestinal disease.

questions.stemHtml: A 6-year-old child presents to the clinic with a 2-day history of rapidly increasing, itchy skin lesions on the face and arms. On examination, the lesions appear as small vesicles with honey-colored crusting. The mother reports that the child started school recently and that similar lesions have appeared in other classmates. What is the most common causative agent of this condition?
questions.solutionHtml:
tyle="font-size:11pt">Option A: Streptococcus pneumoniae typically causes respiratory infections and is not commonly associated with skin infections like impetigo.

 

Option C: Pseudomonas aeruginosa can cause skin infections, particularly in burn wounds or in hot tub folliculitis, but it is not the typical organism for impetigo.

 

Option D: Herpes simplex virus causes herpetic lesions that can be vesicular but do not typically present with honey-colored crusting and are not as rapidly spreading in a community setting like impetigo.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Staphylococcus aureus as the most common causative agent of honey-colored crusted lesions (Impetigo), particularly in the pediatric population and settings like schools where close contact facilitates spread.

 

Ref: Apurva Sastry Essentials of Medical MicrobiologyEssentials of Medical Microbiologypg 514/4e 



Apurva Sastry Essentials of Medical MicrobiologyEssentials of Medical Microbiologypg 514/4e

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man with a history of diabetes and chronic kidney disease presents to the emergency department with fever, hypotension, and a raised white cell count. His skin is warm and flushed, but there is no rash, desquamation, or signs of localized infection. Blood cultures are pending. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis if this patient's condition is not primarily due to a toxin-mediated effect?
questions.solutionHtml:
style="font-size:11pt">Explanation:

 

Option A: Toxic shock syndrome is characterized by fever, rash, desquamation, and hypotension, often associated with tampon use or skin infections but is toxin-mediated, which does not fit the clinical scenario provided.

 

Option B: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome is a toxin-mediated condition that presents with widespread blistering and desquamation of the skin, especially in infants and children.

 

Option C: Staphylococcal food poisoning is also toxin-mediated and would present with rapid onset nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea following ingestion of contaminated food.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The patient's presentation of fever, hypotension, raised white cell count, and absence of rash or localized infection signs, especially in the context of his pre-existing conditions (diabetes and chronic kidney disease), strongly suggests septic shock. Septic shock is a severe infection that leads to organ dysfunction and low blood pressure, not necessarily linked to a toxin-mediated effect like those seen in toxic shock syndrome or staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome.

 

Ref: Apurva Sastry Essentials of Medical Microbiology Essentials of Medical Microbiology pg 514/4e 




Apurva Sastry Essentials of Medical Microbiology Essentials of Medical Microbiology pg 514/4e

questions.stem: In the laboratory, a strain of Staphylococcus aureus is noted to be resistant to methicillin. A medical student is asked to identify the primary mechanism by which this resistance is conveyed. Which of the following best describes the primary resistance mechanism of this bacterium?

options.label: D
options.text: Activation of an efflux pump mechanism

questions.solutionHtml:
n:

 

Option B: Changes in cell wall permeability can lead to antibiotic resistance, but this is not the primary mechanism for methicillin resistance in S. aureus.

 

Option C: Modulation of antibiotic response pathways may contribute to resistance but is not the primary mechanism by which S. aureus exhibits methicillin resistance.

 

Option D: An efflux pump mechanism can cause resistance by actively transporting antibiotics out of the bacterial cell, but this is not the main mechanism of resistance in MRSA.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) resists methicillin primarily through altered penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs), specifically PBP2a, encoded by the mecA gene. This differs from other resistance mechanisms like changes in cell wall permeability or efflux pump activation, highlighting the need for alternative treatments in MRSA infections.

 

Ref: Apurva Sastry Essentials of Medical MicrobiologyEssentials of Medical MicrobiologyChap 3.5 /4e 



Apurva Sastry Essentials of Medical MicrobiologyEssentials of Medical MicrobiologyChap 3.5 /4e

questions.stem: A 12-year-old girl presents with a one-week history of sore throat, fever, and malaise. She now complains of painful, swollen knees and elbows. Physical examination reveals a new heart murmur. Her past medical history is significant for recurrent pharyngitis. The pediatrician is concerned about the development of a post-infectious complication. Which organism is most commonly implicated as a trigger for this patient's condition?
questions.solutionHtml:
="font-family:"Calibri",sans-serif">Explanation:

 

Option A: Alpha-hemolytic Streptococci (including Streptococcus pneumoniae and Streptococcus viridans group) are typically associated with respiratory infections and endocarditis, respectively, but not rheumatic fever.

 

Option C: Gamma-hemolytic Streptococci (non-hemolytic) are not usually associated with invasive disease or post-infectious complications like rheumatic fever.

 

Option D: Staphylococcus aureus can cause a wide range of infections but is not implicated in the etiology of rheumatic fever.

 

Educational Objective:

 

 

Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology 1/e p226, 2/e p232

questions.stem: A 14-year-old male presents with a swollen and painful right knee. His symptoms began two weeks after an untreated sore throat. On examination, his knee is warm, erythematous, and exhibits restricted range of motion. An aspirate of the synovial fluid is obtained, which shows increased white blood cells but no organisms on Gram stain. The pediatrician suspects acute rheumatic fever and explains that certain streptococcal antigens can induce an autoimmune reaction by molecular mimicry. Which streptococcal component is known to cross-react with synovial tissues, contributing to the pathogenesis of this patient's condition?
questions.solutionHtml:
t;Calibri",sans-serif">Explanation:

 

Option B: Cell wall protein: While M protein of Group A Streptococcus is implicated in the immune response, it is not the antigen known for cross-reactivity with synovial fluid.

 

Option C: Capsular hyaluronic acid: Although the capsule of Group A Streptococcus is composed of hyaluronic acid, it is not specifically associated with cross-reactivity in synovial fluid.

 

Option D: Peptidoglycan: This is a structural component of the bacterial cell wall and is not typically involved in the autoimmune response associated with acute rheumatic fever.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The carbohydrate antigen in Group A Streptococcus, particularly the N-acetylglucosamine in its cell wall, can cross-react with human tissues like synovial fluid, leading to acute rheumatic fever. This occurs as antibodies against streptococcal antigens mistakenly target the body's own tissues, causing inflammation and symptoms like arthritis. 

 

Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology 1/e p225, 2/e p232, Ananthanarayan 9/e p212, 10/e p212



Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology 1/e p225, 2/e p232, Ananthanarayan 9/e p212, 10/e p212

questions.stem: An 8-year-old boy presents to the pediatric clinic with fever, malaise, and a painful erythematous lesion on his shin, which he reports developed after falling at the playground. The lesion has a honey-colored crust, and underlying erythema. A Gram stain of the discharge reveals gram-positive cocci in chains, and culture plates demonstrate hemolytic colonies. The physician considers further testing to confirm the specific etiological agent responsible for the skin infection. Which test would be most appropriate to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Explanation:

 

Option A: Bile solubility test: This test is used to differentiate Streptococcus pneumoniae, which is bile soluble, from other alpha-hemolytic streptococci.

 

Option B: Optochin sensitivity test: This test is also used to identify Streptococcus pneumoniae, which is optochin-sensitive, from other viridans group streptococci.

 

Option D: Catalase test: This test distinguishes staphylococci (catalase-positive) from streptococci (catalase-negative). Since we already know the organism is a streptococcus, this test would not be useful in further identification.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The bacitracin sensitivity test is key for identifying Group A Streptococcus (GAS) in suspected skin infections, as GAS shows a distinct zone of inhibition to bacitracin. This differentiates it from other bacteria. Other tests like the bile solubility and optochin sensitivity tests are used for identifying Streptococcus pneumoniae, distinguishing it from other alpha-hemolytic streptococci. The catalase test differentiates staphylococci (catalase-positive) from streptococci (catalase-negative), but it's not helpful for further identification within streptococcal species.

 

Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology 1/e p227, 2/e p234, Ananthanarayan 9/e p215,10/e p217- 218



Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology 1/e p227, 2/e p234, Ananthanarayan 9/e p215,10/e p217- 218

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the clinic with a sore throat, fever, and difficulty swallowing for the past two days. Examination reveals erythema and swelling of the tonsils with exudate. No cough or rhinorrhea is noted. A rapid strep test returns positive. The physician explains to the parents that the condition is caused by a specific pathogen that initiates the disease through a particular process. What is the primary mechanism by which Group A hemolytic streptococci cause pharyngitis in this child?
questions.solutionHtml:
lonize the pharyngeal tissue and elicit an inflammatory response, leading to the symptoms of pharyngitis.

 

Explanation:

 

Option B: Systemic toxicity: While GAS can cause systemic effects, particularly in invasive diseases such as toxic shock syndrome, pharyngitis is primarily a local infection.

 

Option C: Attachment to mucosa: While initial attachment to the mucosa is a step in the pathogenesis of GAS infection, it is not the direct cause of pharyngitis symptoms, which result from the local infection and subsequent inflammatory response.

 

Option D: Production of local toxins: GAS does produce toxins, but the primary symptoms of pharyngitis are not due to the local toxins but rather due to the local infectious process.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Group A beta-hemolytic streptococcus (GAS), or Streptococcus pyogenes, primarily causes pharyngitis through a local infection in the pharyngeal tissue. This infection triggers an inflammatory response, leading to the symptoms associated with pharyngitis. Although GAS can result in systemic effects in more severe diseases and produces toxins, the primary mechanism of pharyngitis is the local infection itself, not systemic toxicity, mere attachment to the mucosa, or the production of local toxins.

 

Ref: Harrison Principles of Internal Medicine19/e p964, 20/e p1082



Harrison Principles of Internal Medicine19/e p964, 20/e p1082

questions.stem: A laboratory researcher is studying the pathogenesis of Staphylococcus aureus and focuses on the toxins that contribute to its virulence. One group of toxins has been noted to have synergistic activity on the polymorphonuclear cells when combined with other staphylococcal hemolysins. Which toxin is known for this synergistic activity?
questions.solutionHtml:
span style="font-size:12.0pt;">Explanation:

 

Option A: Alpha toxin - Alpha toxin, also produced by Staphylococcus aureus, is a pore-forming toxin that causes cell lysis but does not exhibit the same synergistic hemolytic activity as PVL.

 

Option B: Beta toxin - Beta toxin: A sphingomyelinase with activity mainly on RBC membranes, especially sheep RBCs — shows synergy in hemolysis, not on PMNs

 

Option D: Delta toxin - Delta toxin is not a well-known toxin associated with Staphylococcus aureus pathogenesis and does not exhibit synergistic hemolytic activity.

 

Educational Objective:

 

 

Ref: Apurva Sastry Essentials of Medical Microbiology pg 512/4e





Apurva Sastry Essentials of Medical Microbiology pg 512/4e

t">Option B: Staphylococcus aureus is typically resistant to Bacitracin and is not commonly associated with pharyngitis.

Use of Bacitracin sensitivity testing in identifying Streptococcus pyogenes as a cause of pharyngitis and to differentiate it from other potential pathogens based on antibiotic sensitivity patterns. Group A streptococcus is Sensitive while Group B streptococcus is Resistant.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman presents to the clinic with complaints of painful genital ulcers. She has a history of unprotected sexual contact two weeks prior. On examination, the ulcers are soft, with ragged borders and bleed easily upon contact. There is also painful swelling noted in the inguinal region. Based on the clinical presentation, which of the following is the most likely causative organism?
questions.solutionHtml:
Explanation:

 

Option A. Treponema pallidum causes syphilis, which presents with a painless chancre, not consistent with the painful genital ulcers in this case.

 

Option B. Herpes Simplex Virus causes herpes genitalis, which presents with painful vesicles or ulcers, but these are typically not described as having ragged borders and are usually not as easily bleeding as those caused by H. ducreyi.

 

Option D. Chlamydia trachomatis can lead to lymphogranuloma venereum, which does present with genital lesions and lymphadenopathy, but the initial lesion is typically transient and not as painful as chancroid ulcers.

 

Educational Objective:

 

 

Ref:   Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology 1/e p348, 2/e p363, Ananthanarayan 9/e p330, 10/e p337

options.label: C
options.text: Changes in the membrane permeability to penicillin

options.label: D
options.text: Production of an alternative penicillin binding protein

questions.answerText: Production of an alternative penicillin binding protein

>Explanation:

 

Option A: Production of Beta lactamase is a common resistance mechanism in other bacteria but not the primary one in Streptococcus pneumoniae.

 

Option B: Mutations in the proteins on the bacterial surface can contribute to resistance but are not the primary mechanism for penicillin resistance in S. pneumoniae.

 

Option C: Changes in membrane permeability are a less common mechanism of resistance for S. pneumoniae when compared to PBP alterations.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Mechanism of penicillin resistance in Streptococcus pneumoniae is due to the production of altered penicillin-binding proteins, leading to a decreased affinity for the drug.

questions.stem: A patient in the intensive care unit (ICU) with a central venous catheter develops a fever after a week of antibiotic therapy with ceftazidime and amikacin. Blood cultures reveal gram-positive cocci in chains, and the organism is catalase-negative. Vancomycin is initiated, but the patient's blood cultures remain positive for the same organism after two weeks of therapy. Which organism is the most likely cause of this persistent bacteremia?
questions.solutionHtml:
nation:

 

Option A: Staphylococcus aureus is usually catalase-positive, coagulase-positive and gram positive cocci in clusters.

 

Option C: Enterococcus faecalis can cause persistent bacteremia but is usually vancomycin-resistant but is gram positive cocci in pairs.

 

Option D: Coagulase-negative staphylococci are also catalase-positive and would not typically present as cocci in chains.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Viridans group streptococci is a common cause of , bloodstream infections, particularly in patients with icentral venous catheters, and to recognize the challenge of treating biofilm-associated infections that can lead to persistent bacteremia despite appropriate antibiotic therapy.

 

Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology 1/e p 231, 2/e p238

questions.stem: A 45-year-old male with a history of rheumatic heart disease presents with fever, a new heart murmur, and petechiae after a recent dental procedure. Blood cultures are drawn, and empiric antibiotic therapy is initiated. The cultures eventually grow gram-positive cocci that are not encapsulated and are alpha-hemolytic. Which organism is most likely responsible for this patient's infective endocarditis?
questions.solutionHtml:
pan>

 

Option B: Streptococcus pneumoniae, while alpha-hemolytic, is more commonly associated with pneumonia and meningitis rather than endocarditis.

 

Option C: Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A Streptococcus) is beta-hemolytic and is not typically associated with endocarditis following dental procedures.

 

Option D: Staphylococcus aureus can cause acute endocarditis, often in intravenous drug users or in patients with prosthetic valves and is usually beta-hemolytic and coagulase-positive.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Streptococcus viridans is a common etiological agent for infective endocarditis in patients with preexisting valvular heart disease following dental procedures.

Quellung reaction is used to detect the presence of the polysaccharide capsule of Streptococcus pneumoniae, which is an important pathogen in community-acquired pneumonia with characteristic rust-colored sputum.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old male with a history of poorly controlled diabetes mellitus presents to the emergency department with severe pain, redness, and swelling of the lower left leg. He reports a minor abrasion on his leg a few days ago. On examination, the skin is dusky with bullae and crepitus is noted. A diagnosis of necrotizing fasciitis is suspected, and immediate management is discussed. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step in the management of this patient's condition?
questions.solutionHtml:
pan style="font-size:11pt">Explanation:

 

Option B. High-dose intravenous penicillin: While penicillin is part of the antibiotic regimen for necrotizing fasciitis, particularly for group A Streptococcus. It is not the initial step after debridement.

 

Option C. Intravenous clindamycin: Clindamycin is used in the treatment of necrotizing fasciitis due to its ability to inhibit toxin production; however, it is not the first step before debridement.

 

Option D: Oral metronidazole: Metronidazole is used primarily for anaerobic infections and is not typically the first-line treatment for necrotizing fasciitis.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Necrotizing fasciitis, a severe infection of the fascial planes, necessitates immediate surgical intervention. The most crucial step is the surgical removal of necrotic tissue to reduce bacterial load and prevent the infection from spreading. Although antibiotics like high-dose intravenous penicillin, intravenous clindamycin, oral metronidazole, and intravenous vancomycin are important in the treatment regimen, especially for specific bacterial causes, they are adjunctive and follow surgical debridement, not precede it.

 

Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology1/e p225, 2/e p235, Harrison Principles of Internal Medicine19/e p966, 20/e p1086

questions.stem: A patient presents with a history of low-grade fever, petechial rash, and elevated white blood cell count. Considering the possibility of a systemic infectious process, what would be the most appropriate next diagnostic step?
questions.solutionHtml:
anation:


Option A: Broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy - While treating a suspected infection is crucial, it is preferable to identify the causative organism first to guide specific therapy.


Option C: Immediate lumbar puncture - This would be more appropriate if there were signs of meningitis or central nervous system infection, which are not specified in the scenario.


Option D: Complete blood count with differential - While useful, it does not provide as direct evidence of a systemic infection as blood cultures and would not be the immediate next step in this scenario.

 

Educational Objective:

Blood cultures are essential for identifying the causative organism of a systemic infection, especially in cases where bacteremia or sepsis is suspected.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old male presents with a two-week history of dysuria and a clear urethral discharge. He reports no recent sexual contacts and denies any history of similar symptoms. He is afebrile, and a physical examination is unremarkable except for mild urethral erythema. Urine nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae return negative. le="text-align:justify"> 

Option A: C. trachomatis is a common cause of NGU, but it has been ruled out with negative NAATs.

 

Option B: Mycoplasma hominis is not a typical cause of NGU in men.

 

Option C: Treponema pallidum causes syphilis, which usually presents with a chancre during primary infection, not urethritis.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old male presents to the clinic with persistent urethral discharge and dysuria. He had a single unprotected sexual encounter 1 week prior. His symptoms initially improved after receiving a dose of ceftriaxone but have since returned. Examination shows no signs of genital lesions or inguinal lymphadenopathy. Urinalysis is notable for pyuria, and Gram stain of the urethral discharge reveals numerous polymorphonuclear leukocytes and gram-negative intracellular diplococci. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
questions.solutionHtml:
Option B: Penicillin-resistant Neisseria gonorrhoeae - Less likely as the patient initially responded to ceftriaxone, which is effective against most strains of Neisseria gonorrhoeae.
 

Option C: Reinfection with Neisseria gonorrhoeae - Possible, but less likely than a Chlamydia coinfection given the timeframe and initial response to treatment.

 

Option D: Ureaplasma urealyticum infection - While it can cause urethritis, it's less likely in this case given the presence of gram-negative intracellular diplococci, which are more characteristic of gonorrhea.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The primary issue is penicillin-resistant Neisseria gonorrhoeae, indicating drug resistance in the infected strain rather than a case of reinfection. 
  • Symptoms like urethral discharge and the presence of gram-negative intracellular diplococci suggest Gonococcus infection, typically treated with ceftriaxone.
  • Some strains of Neisseria gonorrhoeae show resistance to beta-lactams, either due to beta-lactamase production (PPNG) or altered penicillin-binding proteins. Ceftriaxone resistance is linked to altered PBP2.
  • Reinfection in women may occur in the presence of antibodies to gonococcal OMP (Rmp), but it's not common following treatment. Reinfection is less likely without a new sexual encounter and can usually be treated with ceftriaxone. Ureaplasma urealyticum infection is unlikely in this context due to Gram stain results and lack of pyuria.

 

Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology 1/e p241, 2/e p250, Harrison rinciples of Internal Medicine19/e p1005-07,20/e p1125

questions.stem: A microbiology resident is lecturing on Corynebacterium diphtheriae. She asks the residents which of the following statements regarding the bacterium and its toxin is accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: Every strain of Corynebacterium diphtheriae produces the diphtheria toxin.

options.label: B
options.text: The production of diphtheria toxin is dependent upon the environmental concentration of iron.

options.label: C
options.text: The gene for diphtheria toxin production is plasmid-borne.

options.label: D
options.text: The diphtheria toxin inhibits cyclic AMP (cAMP) production.

questions.answerText: The production of diphtheria toxin is dependent upon the environmental concentration of iron.
questions.solutionHtml:
ptos,sans-serif">Explanation:

 

Option A: Not all strains produce the toxin; only those infected with a bacteriophage that carries the tox gene can produce the diphtheria toxin.

 

Option C: The diphtheria toxin gene (tox) is not plasmid-borne; it is carried by a lysogenic bacteriophage integrated into the bacterium's genome.

 

Option D: The diphtheria toxin does not inhibit cAMP production; it inhibits protein synthesis by inactivating EF-2.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Diphtheria Toxin (DT) - DT consists of two fragments: Fragment A (active unit) and B (binding unit). Fragment B binds to host cell receptors, facilitating entry of Fragment A. Fragment A is internalized into host cells, where it ADP ribosylates elongation factor 2 (EF2). Inhibition of EF2 leads to irreversible inhibition of protein synthesis, resulting in cell death.

alibri",sans-serif">Explanation:

questions.stem: A pediatric infectious disease specialist is consulted for a child with suspected diphtheria. When discussing the disease, which of the following statements is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Diphtheria can cause peripheral nerve palsies during the second and third weeks of illness.

options.label: B
options.text: Erythromycin is an effective treatment option for diphtheria.

options.text: Diphtheria is caused by a gram-negative organism.

Option A: Diphtheria can cause cranial nerve palsies, typically in the second and third weeks due to the effects of the toxin but doesn’t cause the peripheral nerve palsies.

ight:271px; width:300px" />

Option A: Growth on Potassium tellurite medium is a characteristic of C. diphtheriae, but it does not distinguish between toxigenic and non-toxigenic strains.

Option D: Observing cytotoxic effects in tissue culture assays can suggest toxin activity, but the Elek test is the standard method for confirming diphtheria toxin production.

The Elek test confirms toxigenic Corynebacterium diphtheriae by detecting diphtheria toxin production, unlike growth on Potassium tellurite medium or cytotoxic effects in tissue culture assays.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy with a complete vaccination history presents with fever, sore throat, and painful neck swelling. Examination reveals a pseudomembrane on the right tonsil. To rapidly identify the responsible pathogen from a throat swab, which culture medium is most appropriate?

le="font-size:11pt">

Option A: Nutrient agar is not selective and is not the best choice for isolating C. diphtheriae, which requires an enrichment medium.

 

Option B: Blood agar is a general-purpose medium and, although it supports the growth of a wide range of bacteria, it is not specific for isolating C. diphtheriae.

 

Option D: Lowenstein-Jensen medium is specific for mycobacteria, particularly Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and is not suitable for C. diphtheriae.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Loffler's serum slope is the preferred culture medium for rapidly identifying Corynebacterium diphtheriae from throat swabs, as it enhances the bacterium's growth more effectively than nutrient or blood agar, or Lowenstein-Jensen medium.

questions.stem: A physician suspects that a patient may be an asymptomatic carrier of Corynebacterium diphtheriae after a close contact developed diphtheria. Which diagnostic method should be utilized to confirm the carrier state in the suspected patient?

edia such as Loffler's or Tinsdale agar is used to identify the presence of C. diphtheriae.

Option D: The Schick's test is a historical test that was used to determine susceptibility to diphtheria toxin, not to diagnose carriers.

 

Educational Objective:

 

To confirm a suspected asymptomatic carrier of Corynebacterium diphtheriae, a throat culture is the most reliable diagnostic method. Other techniques like Gram's staining, Albert's stain, or Schick's test don't specifically identify carrier status or toxin production.

questions.stem: A medical student is reviewing a case study of a patient diagnosed with anthrax. Which of the following statements about anthrax is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: It is caused by Gram-positive bacilli.

options.label: B
options.text: It has a natural reservoir in the soil.

options.label: C
options.text: Spore formation occurs inside the human body.

options.label: D
options.text: It is more commonly found in carnivorous animals than herbivores.

questions.answerText: It is caused by Gram-positive bacilli.
questions.solutionHtml:
2.0pt">Anthrax is caused by Bacillus anthracis, which is a Gram-positive, rod-shaped bacterium.

 

Explanation:

 

Option B: While B. anthracis spores are found in the soil, this statement is not a complete descriptor of the disease's ecology.

 

Option C: Spore formation does not take place inside the body; it occurs when the bacterium is exposed to air outside the host.

 

Option D: Anthrax is more common in herbivorous animals, as they are more likely to ingest spores while grazing.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Anthrax is caused by the Gram-positive bacillus Bacillus anthracis. The disease is more common in herbivores and its spores are found in soil. Spore formation occurs outside the body, and ciprofloxacin or doxycycline are preferred over penicillin for treatment due to resistance concerns.

questions.stem: A surgeon discusses the pathophysiology of gas gangrene with medical students. He explains several factors that contribute to the development of this condition. Which of the following statements is true regarding gas gangrene?

options.label: A
options.text: The primary toxin associated with the toxemia seen in gas gangrene is α-toxin.

options.label: B
options.text: It is mainly caused by Clostridium intestinale.

options.label: C
options.text: The presence of high oxygen tension in tissue is a crucial predisposing factor.

options.label: D
options.text: The condition is predisposed by the presence of vital tissue.

questions.answerText: The primary toxin associated with the toxemia seen in gas gangrene is α-toxin.
questions.solutionHtml:
> 

Explanation:

 

Option B: This statement is incorrect as Clostridium intestinale is not a common causative organism of gas gangrene.

 

Option C: This statement is incorrect: Low oxygen tension in tissue is a predisposing factor for gas gangrene not high oxygen.

 

Option D: This statement is incorrect: The presence of devitalized tissue is crucial predisposing factor not vital tissue for gas gangrene.

 

Educational Objective: 

 

Gas gangrene is mainly caused by Clostridium perfringens, which produces α-toxin (lecithinase), the primary toxin responsible for toxemia and tissue destruction in this condition. Other factors, such as the presence of devitalized tissue and low oxygen tension in the tissue, also contribute to its development. Gas gangrene occurs when dead tissue is present, and it is not associated with Clostridium intestinale.

questions.stem: A public health officer is reviewing cases of bacterial infections in a community and notes several reports of neonatal meningitis. Which of the following bacteria is the least likely to be a protective vaccine target due to the lack of a polysaccharide capsule?
questions.solutionHtml:
Explanation:

 

Option A. Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) vaccine targets the polysaccharide capsule and is effective in preventing Hib infections, including meningitis.

 

Option B. Neisseria meningitidis vaccines target the polysaccharide capsule of different serogroups, providing protection against meningococcal meningitis.

 

Option C. Streptococcus pneumoniae vaccines, such as the pneumococcal conjugate vaccine, target the polysaccharide capsule and are effective in preventing invasive pneumococcal disease.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Bordetella pertussis, the bacterium responsible for whooping cough, is unique among the options as it lacks a polysaccharide capsule, making its vaccine strategy different. Unlike Haemophilus influenzae type b, Neisseria meningitidis, and Streptococcus pneumoniae, which all have polysaccharide capsules targeted by their respective vaccines, B. pertussis vaccines are acellular. These contain purified bacterial components but not the polysaccharide capsule, as it doesn't possess one.

Explanation:

 

Option A: True, Clostridium tetani produces heat-resistant spores, which can survive in the environment for long periods.

 

Option B: True, tetanus cannot be transmitted from person to person; it is acquired through environmental exposure to the spores of the bacterium.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old boy with a history of complete primary immunization and a booster given 6 years ago is brought to the emergency room with a contaminated wound on his left leg from a road traffic accident. Which of the following interventions is NOT indicated in this scenario?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Administer human tetanus immune globulin. 

 

The patient had complete primary immunization and a booster 6 years ago.
 

For contaminated wounds, TT booster is indicated if last dose was >5 years ago, but immunoglobulin is not needed if the patient has had ≥3 doses of tetanus vaccine.

 

Other Options:
 

Option A: Administer a tetanus toxoid (TT) booster: Needed as last immunization was 6 Years ago.

 

Option C: Prescribe broad-spectrum antibiotics: Indicated for contaminated wound to prevent secondary bacterial infections.

 

Option D. Perform wound debridement and cleaning: This is a first-line step in all tetanus-prone wounds — removes necrotic tissue and dirt.
 

Educational Objective:

 

Prevention of Tetanus in Wound

 

Where,

 

A. Complete course of toxoid or booster dose in previous 5 years

 

B. Complete course of toxoid or booster dose in previous 5-10 years

 

C. Complete course of toxoid or booster dose in >10 years ago

 

D. Has not had a complete course of toxoid or status is unknown.

questions.stem: A trauma patient is admitted to the hospital with concerns for gas gangrene due to a deep, necrotizing wound sustained in a farming accident. Which of the following statements is correct regarding gas gangrene?

options.label: A
options.text: The underlying skin and muscles typically appear normal.

options.label: B
options.text: It is caused by the tetanospasmin toxin.

options.label: C
options.text: The condition is characterized by muscle rigidity and spasms.

options.label: D
options.text: The most commonly implicated organism in gas gangrene is Clostridium perfringens.

questions.answerText: The most commonly implicated organism in gas gangrene is Clostridium perfringens.
questions.solutionHtml:
cularly type A, is the most frequent cause of gas gangrene, a severe form of necrotizing soft tissue infection.

 

Explanation:

 

Option A: False, in gas gangrene, there is often severe damage to the skin and muscles, which is not normal.

 

Option B: False, gas gangrene is not caused by tetanospasmin toxin, which is associated with tetanus, not gas gangrene.

 

Option C: False, muscle rigidity and spasms are more characteristic of tetanus; gas gangrene typically causes severe pain, swelling, and production of gas.

 

 

Educational Objective:

 

Gas gangrene, also known as clostridial myonecrosis, is most commonly caused by Clostridium perfringens, a gram-positive, anaerobic bacterium. This condition often results from deep, traumatic wounds, especially in environments contaminated with soil or feces where the bacteria are commonly found. Gas gangrene is characterized by rapid tissue necrosis, gas production in tissues, and systemic toxicity. It is a medical emergency requiring prompt surgical and medical intervention.

Ans. B) Administer a booster dose of tetanus toxoid. 

 

Option B:

 

For individuals with a complete primary immunization who sustain a clean, minor wound, a booster dose of tetanus toxoid is recommended if more than 10 years have elapsed since the last dose.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Prevention of Tetanus in Wound

 

 

 

Where,

 

A. Complete course of toxoid or booster dose in previous 5 years

 

B. Complete course of toxoid or booster dose in previous 5-10 years

 

C. Complete course of toxoid or booster dose in >10 years ago

 

D. Has not had a complete course of toxoid or status is unknown.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding Clostridium tetani?

options.label: A
options.text: The main reservoir for Clostridium tetani is soil, as well as human and animal intestines.

options.label: B
options.text: The most common mode of transmission is through trauma and contaminated wounds.

options.label: C
options.text: Herd immunity is not a useful concept for tetanus prevention.

options.label: D
options.text: The most common season for tetanus cases is winter and in dry conditions.

questions.answerText: The most common season for tetanus cases is winter and in dry conditions.
questions.solutionHtml:
Explanation:

 

Option A, B, and C: all 3 statements are correct 

 

Educational Objective:

 

Tetanus cases do not have a specific seasonal pattern like some other infectious diseases. The occurrence of tetanus is more related to the exposure to Clostridium tetani spores, which are ubiquitous in the environment, especially in soil, and not particularly influenced by seasonal changes. 

 

Clostridium tetani's main reservoirs include soil and the intestines of humans and animals; the bacterium is typically transmitted through contaminated wounds; and herd immunity is not applicable to tetanus prevention since it is not a contagious disease.

 

Ref: Park 23/e p312, 24/e p330

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) There is no period of communicability. 

 

Option D:

 

Tetanus is not contagious and cannot be transmitted from person to person. It is acquired through environmental exposure to the spores of Clostridium tetani.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Tetanus is not a communicable disease and does not have a period of communicability.

questions.stem: During a review of hospital-acquired infections, a case is presented of a 65-year-old man who developed diarrhea after a two-week course of antibiotics for pneumonia. What is the most significant risk factor for the development of his Clostridium difficile infection?

options.label: B
options.text: Use of proton pump inhibitors like pantoprazole

questions.solutionHtml:
p>

 

Explanation:

 

Option B: While proton pump inhibitors are associated with a slightly increased risk of C. difficile infection, they are not as significant a risk factor as antibiotic use.

 

Option C: Use of rectal thermometers has not been established as a risk factor for C. difficile infection.

 

Option D: Although a longer hospital stay may be associated with a higher risk of acquiring C. difficile, it is the antibiotic use during the stay that is the direct risk factor.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The prolonged antibiotic therapy as a significant risk factor for the development of Clostridium difficile infection due to disruption of normal gut flora

Option C: Fried rice is commonly associated with Bacillus cereus food poisoning, not C. difficile infection.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Clostridium difficile is usually linked to extended antibiotic use and hospitalization. The most common antibiotics are cephalosporins, clindamycin, ampicillin, and fluoroquinolones.

questions.stem: A teaching hospital is conducting a seminar on Clostridium difficile infections. The presenter makes several statements about pseudomembranous colitis. Which of the following statements is incorrect?

options.label: A
options.text: Toxin A contributes to clinical manifestations.

options.label: B
options.text: Toxin B contributes to clinical manifestations.

options.label: C
options.text: The presence of blood in the stool is a common finding.

options.label: D
options.text: Summit lesions are observed as an early histopathological feature.

questions.answerText: The presence of blood in the stool is a common finding.
questions.solutionHtml:
ery diarrhea; blood in the stool is not a common feature.

 

Explanation:

 

Option A: Toxin A is indeed responsible for clinical manifestations of pseudomembranous colitis.

 

Option B: Toxin B also contributes to the clinical manifestations of pseudomembranous colitis.

 

Option D: Summit lesions, which are areas of raised yellowish-white plaques, are an early histopathological finding in pseudomembranous colitis.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The presence of blood in the stool is not a common finding in pseudomembranous colitis caused by Clostridium difficile. While diarrhea, often watery, and abdominal pain are hallmark symptoms, significant blood in the stool is not typically a feature of this infection.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old female patient is diagnosed with pseudomembranous colitis. She has a history of penicillin allergy. Which of the following treatments is most appropriate for this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
bsp;

Option B: Penicillin is contraindicated due to the patient's allergy.

 

Option C: Oral ampicillin is not effective against Clostridium difficile.

 

Option D: Clindamycin is one of the antibiotics that can precipitate pseudomembranous colitis and should be avoided.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Treatment for pseudomembranous colitis, especially in the context of a penicillin allergy – 

 

  •  Initial episode, mild to moderate cases: Oral metronidazole is the drug of choice
  • Recurrent episodes or severe cases: Vancomycin is the drug of choice
  •  Severe complicated or fulminant infection: Vancomycin plus IV metronidazole

questions.stem: A 30-year-old male with no history of prior immunization presents to the clinic with a clean, superficial wound incurred two hours prior while working in a garden. He has never received any doses of tetanus toxoid in his lifetime. What is the appropriate tetanus prophylaxis in this situation?

options.label: A
options.text: Begin a full course of tetanus toxoid vaccination

options.label: B
options.text: Administer a single dose of tetanus toxoid

options.label: D
options.text: Administer human tetanus immunoglobulin and a single dose of tetanus toxoid

questions.answerText: Begin a full course of tetanus toxoid vaccination
questions.solutionHtml:
three doses are required to induce adequate immunity.

 

Option C. No intervention is required: This is incorrect because the patient has no prior immunization history. Tetanus prophylaxis is mandatory in such patients, even with a clean wound, to ensure immunity against tetanus.

 

Option D. Administer human tetanus immunoglobulin and a single dose of tetanus toxoid: TIG is only recommended for dirty or high-risk wounds in unvaccinated individuals. In this case, the wound is clean, so TIG is not necessary. 

 

Educational Objective:

 

Prevention of Tetanus in Wound

 

 

Where,

 

A. Complete course of toxoid or booster dose in previous 5 years

 

B. Complete course of toxoid or booster dose in previous 5-10 years

 

C. Complete course of toxoid or booster dose in >10 years ago

 

D. Has not had a complete course of toxoid or status is unknown.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man with a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is hospitalized for an acute exacerbation and treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics. Ten days into his hospital stay, he develops watery diarrhea 3-4 times daily. There is no blood or mucus in the stool, and he has no fever. The stool odor is not foul-smelling. Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic test to confirm Clostridium difficile infection in this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Stool immunofluorescence for C. difficile antigens

options.label: B
options.text: Stool enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) for C. difficile toxins

options.label: C
options.text: Stool polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for C. difficile toxin genes

questions.answerText: Stool polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for C. difficile toxin genes
questions.solutionHtml:
/span>

 

Explanation:

 

Option A: Immunofluorescence for C. difficile antigens is less commonly used due to lower sensitivity compared to PCR.

 

Option B: ELISA for C. difficile toxins has been largely replaced by PCR due to lower sensitivity and specificity.

 

Option D: Stool culture for C. difficile is highly sensitive but less specific and takes longer, making it less ideal for initial diagnosis.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Clostridium difficile infection (CDI) in stool polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for C. difficile toxin genes . This method is highly sensitive and specific, making it the most suitable choice for diagnosing CDI, particularly in patients with recent antibiotic exposure and CDI symptoms. Immunofluorescence for C. difficile antigens  is less commonly used due to its lower sensitivity. ELISA for C. difficile toxins is also less favored due to lower sensitivity and specificity. Stool culture for C. difficile  is highly sensitive but less specific and time-consuming, making it less suitable for initial diagnosis.

 

Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Med Microbiology 1/e p266, 2/e p276



erred diagnostic test for C. difficile infection (CDI), especially in a patient with recent antibiotic exposure and symptoms consistent with CDI.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old male presents to the clinic with a chronic wound on his neck that has been draining pus for several weeks. He denies any fever or significant pain. Physical examination reveals a sinus tract with yellowish granules in the discharge. He has a history of dental procedures and poor oral hygiene. A specimen from the draining material is anaerobic. Which organism is most likely responsible for this presentation?
questions.solutionHtml:
n>

 

Option B: Nocardia asteroides - Nocardia are aerobic actinomycetes that can cause cutaneous infections but typically do not form sulfur granules.

 

Option C: Salmonella typhi - Salmonella typhi causes typhoid fever, which does not present with draining sinuses or sulfur granules.

 

Option D: Francisella tularensis - This is the causative agent of tularemia, which can cause ulceroglandular disease but does not typically produce sulfur granules.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Actinomyces israelii as the likely causative agent in chronic wound infections presenting with sinus tracts and sulfur granules, particularly in individuals with a history of dental issues and poor oral hygiene

The characteristic branching filaments of Actinomyces species as the likely causative agent of chronic mandibular infections presenting with sulfur granules and draining sinuses.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with a history of aortic valve replacement presents with signs of infective endocarditis. Blood cultures grow gram-positive cocci that are not completely hemolytic. Susceptibility testing indicates that the organism is resistant to penicillin, but synergistic bactericidal activity is observed when penicillin is combined with an aminoglycoside. Which organism is most likely responsible for the infection?
questions.solutionHtml:
ly:"Calibri",sans-serif">Option B: Staphylococcus aureus is also a common cause of endocarditis but does not require combination therapy with penicillin and an aminoglycoside for treatment.

 

Option C: Streptococcus pneumoniae can cause pneumonia and meningitis but is not commonly associated with infective endocarditis and does not require aminoglycoside synergy.

 

Option D: Bacteroides fragilis is an anaerobic bacterium that is not typically involved in endocarditis and does not require aminoglycoside synergy.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Most common agent in specific types of endocarditis

 

  • Native valve endocarditis: Staphylococcus aureus
  • Community acquired—Viridans streptococci
  • Healthcare acquired—S. Aureus
  • Prosthetic valve endocarditis: 
    • Early (occurs within 12 months of valve replacement)—Staphylococcus epidermidis (MC)
    • Late (occurs after 12 months of valve replacement)— Viridans streptococci (MC)
       
  • Endocarditis in IV drug abusers: 
    • Right sided: Staphylococcus aureus  (MC)
    • Left sided: MEnterococcus  (MC), followed by S. aureus 
       
  • Overall: Most common agent is Staphylococcus aureus

Option D. O104:H21 - This serotype is not commonly associated with hemorrhagic colitis or HUS.

E. coli O157:H7 as the serotype most frequently associated with hemorrhagic colitis following consumption of undercooked ground beef.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old male presents with a firm swelling of the jaw that has been progressively enlarging over several months. He reports a dull ache in the area and occasional drainage of pus from small openings in the skin. Examination reveals a woody-hard, non-tender mass with several draining sinuses on the left side of the jaw. Histopathological examination of the exudate reveals filamentous organisms that are not acid-fast. What is the most accurate statement regarding the causative organism?

options.label: A

options.label: C
options.text: Detection in clinical specimens is best achieved with fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH).

questions.stemHtml: A 38-year-old woman presents for her routine gynecological examination. She has an intrauterine device (IUD) for contraception and reports no significant medical history. On examination, her Pap smear reveals small clusters of bacteria associated with squamous cells, without any signs of cellular atypia or viral cytopathic effects.(see figure). There are no protozoans or yeast cells identified. Given this finding, which organism is most likely present on the Pap smear?

options.label: A
options.text: Trichomonas vaginalis, indicating a protozoan infection

options.label: B
options.text: Candida species, suggestive of a yeast infection

options.label: C
options.text: Herpes simplex virus Type II, indicative of a viral infection

options.label: D
options.text: Actinomyces species, associated with IUD use

questions.answerText: Actinomyces species, associated with IUD use
questions.solutionHtml:
pan style="font-size:12.0pt">Explanation:

 

Option A: Trichomonas vaginalis - This protozoan infection typically shows flagellated protozoans on wet mount and not on a Pap smear.

 

Option B: Candida species - Candida yeast infections are usually identified on Pap smears by the presence of pseudohyphae or budding yeasts.

 

Option C: Herpes simplex virus Type II - Herpes infection is characterized by the presence of multinucleated giant cells and cells with ground-glass nuclei, which are not described in the presented scenario.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The presence of small bacterial clusters associated with squamous cells on a Pap smear in a woman with an IUD is indicative of Actinomyces species. Actinomyces are bacteria that can be associated with long-term IUD use and can lead to actinomycosis, a rare but potentially serious infection. This finding warrants further investigation and possibly the removal of the IUD.

 

Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology/p292-93

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease presents with a cough and weight loss. A chest CT scan shows a cavitary lesion in the right upper lobe. Sputum culture grows branching filamentous organisms. Which of the following statements is accurate regarding the characteristics of the organisms that might be isolated from this patient?

options.label: A

options.label: B

options.label: C

questions.answerText: Both can exist as normal flora in the human body and cause opportunistic infections.

trong>Both are strict anaerobes and commonly associated with dental abscesses - Nocardia is an obligate aerobe, not an anaerobe, and while Actinomyces can cause dental abscesses, Nocardia typically does not.

 

Option C: Both organisms exhibit acid-fastness due to the presence of mycolic acids in their cell walls -  Nocardia exhibits partial acid-fastness due to the presence of mycolic acids, but Actinomyces does not.

 

Option D: Infections caused by these organisms are exclusively seen in immunocompromised hosts - Actinomyces can cause infection in both immunocompetent and immunocompromised hosts.

 

Educational Objective:

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with acute onset of a high fever, a sore throat, and difficulty swallowing. Examination reveals a grayish-white membrane on her tonsils and pharynx. Which of the following organisms is most likely to be recovered from the pharyngeal membrane of this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Actinomyces israelii, associated with chronic infection with sulfur granules

options.label: B
options.text: Group A Streptococcus, commonly implicated in pharyngitis and rheumatic fever

options.label: C
options.text: Neisseria meningitidis, associated with petechial rashes and meningococcemia

options.label: D

questions.answerText: Corynebacterium diphtheriae, known for causing diphtheria with pseudomembrane formation

2px; width:400px" />

 

Explanation:

 

Option A: Actinomyces israelii - This organism causes chronic granulomatous infections and is not typically associated with acute pharyngitis and pseudomembrane formation.

 

Option B: Group A Streptococcus - While this bacterium can cause pharyngitis, it does not produce the classic pseudomembrane associated with diphtheria.

 

Option C: Neisseria meningitidis - This organism is associated with meningococcemia and a petechial rash, not pseudomembrane formation in the throat.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Corynebacterium diphtheriae as the causative agent of diphtheria, which presents with a characteristic pseudomembrane in the throat, and differentiate it from other organisms that cause pharyngitis or systemic infections.

questions.stem: A dairy farmer, a 50-year-old male, presents to the clinic complaining of intermittent fever for the past two weeks. He has a low-grade fever that spikes in the evening, along with associated muscle aches and a mild headache. He mentions consuming homemade cheese from his cows' unpasteurized milk. A blood culture is performed, showing small, gram-positive rods capable of tumbling motility at room temperature. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
="font-family:"Calibri",sans-serif">Explanation:

 

Option A: Bovine tuberculosis - Caused by Mycobacterium bovis, it typically does not present with tumbling motility in gram-positive rods.

 

Option C: Brucellosis - While also associated with unpasteurized milk, Brucella species are small gram-negative coccobacilli, and do not exhibit tumbling motility.

 

Option D: Anthrax - Caused by Bacillus anthracis, it can be associated with occupational exposure in farmers but is characterized by large, gram-positive rods in chains, not tumbling motility.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Listeriosis, is a food-borne pathogen that poses a significant risk, especially to neonates, pregnant women, and the elderly. Transmission occurs primarily through contaminated food, vertical transmission (mother to fetus during birth), and is common in aged soft cheeses, packaged meats, milk, and salads due to its ability to survive refrigeration.

 

Listeriosis is most prevalent in extremes of age and is more likely in individuals using proton pump inhibitors or with compromised immunity. 

 

Ref: Apurba Sastry's Essentials of Medical Microbiology/p296



rigeration.

questions.stem: During a prenatal visit, a 32-year-old woman in her second trimester of pregnancy is counseled about food safety. The physician emphasizes the risk of contracting certain foodborne illnesses that could affect her and her unborn child. The physician discusses a specific gram-positive bacterium that can cause severe neonatal infection and is often contracted through the consumption of contaminated deli meats and unpasteurized dairy products. Which of the following statements is true regarding the infection risk and management of this organism?

options.label: A
options.text: Pregnant women have a lower risk of infection compared to the general population.

options.label: B
options.text: Newborns are not susceptible to serious disease caused by this organism.

options.label: C
options.text: The elderly are not considered a high-risk group for infection by this organism.

options.label: D
options.text: Ampicillin is generally the first-line treatment for infections caused by this organism.

questions.answerText: Ampicillin is generally the first-line treatment for infections caused by this organism.
questions.solutionHtml:
n style="font-family:Aptos,sans-serif">Explanation:

 

Option A: Pregnant women have a lower risk of infection compared to the general population - This is incorrect; pregnant women are at a higher risk of contracting listeriosis and can transmit the infection to the fetus.

 

Option B: Newborns are not susceptible to serious disease caused by this organism - This is incorrect; neonates can contract listeriosis from their mothers and are at risk of severe infection.

 

Option C: The elderly are not considered a high-risk group for infection by this organism - This is incorrect; the elderly, particularly those with weakened immune systems, are at higher risk for severe disease.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Listeriosis - Ampicillin is the drug of choice for treating Listeria meningitis, while Amoxicillin is recommended for febrile gastroenteritis in vulnerable populations, but cephalosporins and chloramphenicol should be avoided.

 

Ref: Apurba Sastry's Essentials of Medical Microbiology/p297, 2/e p308

questions.stem: A 70-year-old male with a history of diabetes mellitus and chronic renal failure is admitted with confusion, headache, and a stiff neck. His symptoms started 3 days ago and have progressively worsened. His family reports he frequently consumes deli meats from a local vendor. A lumbar puncture reveals an elevated white cell count with a predominance of neutrophils, low glucose, and high protein. Gram-positive rods are noted on the CSF gram stain. What is the treatment of choice for the suspected pathogen in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
n is the drug of choice, high doses (2 g IV every 4 h)

 

Explanation:

 

Option B: Amoxicillin - While amoxicillin is active against Listeria, it is not the preferred treatment for Listeria meningitis; ampicillin has better central nervous system penetration.

 

Option C: Vancomycin - Vancomycin is not the first-line treatment for Listeria; it is more typically used for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) or penicillin-resistant pneumococci.

 

Option D: Amikacin - Amikacin may be used in combination with ampicillin for synergy against Listeria, but it is not used as monotherapy.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The presence of gram-positive rods in the CSF gram stain indicate bacterial meningitis, likely caused by Listeria monocytogenes. Ampicillin is the preferred treatment for Listeria meningitis, particularly effective in high-risk groups like the elderly, immunocompromised individuals, or pregnant women. While amoxicillin is active against Listeria, ampicillin is favored for its better CNS penetration. 

 

Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology 1/e p296, 2/e p308, Harrison Principles of Internal Medicine19/e p982-83, 20/e p1102



erred treatment for Listeria meningitis; ampicillin has better central nervous system penetration.

options.label: A
options.text: It is the most commonly isolated anaerobe in clinical specimens.

options.label: B
options.text: It has uniform sensitivity to metronidazole.

options.label: C

options.label: D
options.text: Shock and disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) are commonly associated with Bacteroides bacteremia.

questions.answerText: Shock and disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) are commonly associated with Bacteroides bacteremia.
questions.solutionHtml:
="font-family:"Calibri",sans-serif">Explanation:

 

Option A: B. fragilis is indeed the most frequently isolated anaerobe from clinical samples.

 

Option B: B. fragilis is generally sensitive to metronidazole, making the statement false.

 

Option C: The lipopolysaccharide of B. fragilis is structurally and functionally different from conventional endotoxin, which is true.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Bacteroides fragilis:

 

  • Non-sporing anaerobe, capsulated gram-negative bacilli
  • MC commensal in human intestine
  • MC anaerobe to cause infection, causes abdominal infection
  • Endotoxin is less toxic than that of aerobic gram-negative bacilli

questions.stem: A 28-year-old pregnant woman at 30 weeks gestation presents to the emergency department with a 24-hour history of fever, muscle aches, and nausea. She reports eating soft cheeses and deli meats in the past week. Blood cultures are drawn and empirically treated for suspected sepsis. The cultures grow a gram-positive rod that demonstrates tumbling motility at room temperature. Which of the following characteristics is incorrect regarding the organism isolated?

options.label: B
options.text: Typically presents with meningitis in neonates and immunocompromised individuals

options.label: D
options.text: Displays tumbling motility when observed under a microscope

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Considered a gram-negative coccobacillus. 

 

Option C:

 

Listeria monocytogenes is a gram-positive rod, not gram-negative, and it is not a coccobacillus. 

 

The clinical scenario provided suggests a foodborne illness with a typical presentation and risk factors for listeriosis. The tumbling motility, enhanced growth at cold temperatures (cold enrichment), and risk of meningitis in neonates are all classic characteristics of Listeria monocytogenes.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A: Exhibits enhanced growth at 4°C (cold enrichment) - This is a true characteristic of Listeria as it can replicate at refrigerator temperatures, which is a unique feature among pathogens.

 

Option B: Typically presents with meningitis in neonates and immunocompromised individuals - This is also true. Listeriosis can cause severe infections such as meningitis, especially in high-risk groups such as neonates, pregnant women, and immunocompromised individuals.

 

Option D: Displays tumbling motility when observed under a microscope - This is a true characteristic. The tumbling motility is due to the organism's flagellar movement and is a diagnostic clue in the laboratory identification of Listeria.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Listeria monocytogenes, is a food-borne pathogen that poses a significant risk, especially to neonates, pregnant women, and the elderly. Transmitted primarily through contaminated food, vertical transmission (mother to fetus during birth), and is common in aged soft cheeses, packaged meats, milk, and salads due to its ability to survive refrigeration. 

 

Ampicillin is the drug of choice

 

Ref: Apurba Sastry's Essentials of Medical Microbiology 1/e p296, 2/e p308

questions.stem: A 28-year-old male with a productive cough, night sweats, and weight loss for the past 3 weeks is suspected of having pulmonary tuberculosis. Which of the following is the most definitive diagnostic test for confirming Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection in this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) for M. tuberculosis DNA

options.label: C
options.text: Culture of sputum on Lowenstein-Jensen medium

questions.answerText: Culture of sputum on Lowenstein-Jensen medium
questions.solutionHtml:
ily:Aptos,sans-serif"> 

Option A. Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) for M. tuberculosis DNA: Incorrect because, while PCR is rapid and sensitive, it does not replace the definitive culture diagnosis and can sometimes yield false-positive results due to contamination.

 

Option B. Fluorescent staining with Auramine O: Incorrect because, although it is a sensitive method for initial screening, it is not definitive without culture confirmation.

 

Option D. Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR): Incorrect because an elevated ESR is non-specific and not diagnostic for tuberculosis.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The culture of sputum on Lowenstein-Jensen medium is the most definitive diagnostic test for Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection.

t-family:"Calibri",sans-serif">Option B. Edward Jenner: Incorrect. he is known for developing the smallpox vaccine.

Option D. Jonas Salk: Incorrect. he developed the first effective polio vaccine.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Robert Koch as the microbiologist who discovered the tuberculosis bacillus, which was a pivotal moment in the history of infectious disease and microbiology.

Mycobacterium fortuitum is a cause of localized abscess formation following intradermal injections due to its rapid growth and environmental ubiquity.

questions.stem: A neonate is born to a mother with a poorly characterized febrile illness during the third trimester. The infant presents with fever, irritability, and a bulging fontanelle. Blood cultures are drawn, and a lumbar puncture reveals gram-positive rods. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.label: A
options.text: Neonatal sepsis due to Group B Streptococcus

options.label: B
options.text: Neonatal meningitis due to Listeria monocytogenes

options.label: C
options.text: Neonatal tetanus due to Clostridium tetani

options.label: D
options.text: Cutaneous anthrax due to Bacillus anthracis

questions.answerText: Neonatal meningitis due to Listeria monocytogenes
questions.solutionHtml:
span>Group B Streptococcus is a common cause of neonatal sepsis and meningitis, but the CSF Gram stain showing rods rather than cocci is more indicative of Listeria.

 

Option C: Neonatal tetanus presents with muscle rigidity and spasms, not typically with a bulging fontanelle or fever.

 

Option D: Cutaneous anthrax presents with skin lesions, not as neonatal meningitis.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Neonatal meningitis - Gam-positive rods in the CSF of a neonate with consistent clinical findings is suggestive of  Listeria monocytogenes infection

Enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC) - This strain often leads to bloody diarrhea, which the patient does not have. Additionally, the absence of Shiga toxin makes EHEC less likely.

 

Option C: Enteropathogenic E. coli (EPEC) - More commonly associated with persistent diarrhea in infants and is not the leading cause of traveler's diarrhea.

Option C. Enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC) - ETEC causes traveler's diarrhea and is not typically associated with HUS.

 

Option D. Streptococcus pneumoniae - While S. pneumoniae can be associated with HUS, it is not the most common cause in the context of a developing country and bloody diarrhea.

Shigella dysenteriae type 1 as a common cause of HUS in developing countries, particularly following dysentery.

Her mother reports that the child seems very tired and has had a few episodes of unexplained bruising. Laboratory studies show anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury. Which of the following statements about her likely diagnosis is incorrect?

questions.stem: A research laboratory is investigating an outbreak of gastrointestinal infections in a local community. They have isolated a strain of E. coli that seems to be implicated in the illness. The patients present with fever, abdominal cramping, and bloody diarrhea. The researchers decide to perform a test involving the inoculation of the conjunctiva of a guinea pig to observe for the development of keratoconjunctivitis as part of their pathogenicity testing. Which type of E. coli are they most likely attempting to identify with this test?
questions.solutionHtml:
ont-family:Aptos,sans-serif">Option A. Enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC) - This causes watery diarrhea and does not typically involve invasion of the gut mucosa.

 

Option B. Enteropathogenic E. coli (EPEC) - Causes watery diarrhea especially in children, and does not invade cells as EIEC does.

 

Option C. Enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC) - While it can cause bloody diarrhea, it does not invade cells in the same manner as EIEC.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Sereny test is used to identify Enteroinvasive E. coli (EIEC) by demonstrating its ability to cause keratoconjunctivitis in guinea pigs, indicative of its invasive properties.

Urinalysis shows pyuria, bacteriuria, and a positive leukocyte esterase test. A urine culture is pending. Based on the clinical presentation, which organism is the most likely cause of her acute pyelonephritis?
